lines: Welcome to Module Two: Agent Development.
This is where designs become working code, and where agents quietly break.
Picture a travel startup launching a booking assistant.
It searches flights, checks hotels, and books trips, all through tools the model can call.
Its tools were written in a hurry, each with one vague line of description.
So a customer asks for a Lisbon hotel, and the model calls flight search.
Even with the right tool, the model guesses the arguments.
It sends the date as next Friday-ish, and the system just replies: bad request.
The app needs clean JSON to draw the booking screen.
But sometimes the model wraps it in friendly chatter, and the page crashes.
Every hotel search dumps pages of raw data into the conversation.
By step eight, the assistant has forgotten the customer's budget.
Then a booking times out, and the agent tries again.
But the first one went through, so a family pays twice.
The team's only test checks for one exact sentence.
Any harmless rewording breaks it, so nobody trusts it.
The fix wasn't a bigger model.
It was treating tools, outputs, and context as contracts.
Lesson one is tool design: descriptions that say when not to use a tool, plus strict schemas.
And idempotency keys make a retried booking charge only once.
Lesson two is structured output.
Asking for JSON makes errors unlikely, but constrained decoding makes invalid output impossible.
Lesson three maps the frameworks, like LangGraph for stateful agents that pause for human approval.
And NVIDIA's NeMo Agent Toolkit, which wraps them with profiling, evaluation, and tracing.
Lesson four is context engineering: deciding what belongs in the window at each step.
Raw results become short digests, and a stable prompt prefix keeps each step fast and cheap.
Lesson five tests properties, not exact strings: the right tool, valid arguments, within budget.
Each case runs several times, and traces show which stage failed.
This domain is fifteen percent of the exam, and its favourite trap: a schema guarantees a well-formed call, not a correct one.
Lesson one starts right there, with tool design.
